# How to Prepare for a Job Interview Using a Pasted Job Post

> **In short:** Paste a job listing and a short note about your background into your AI assistant, and you'll come away with ten likely interview questions, two talking points for each, and five thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer — typically in under ten minutes of back-and-forth.

A good interview answer sounds rehearsed without sounding rehearsed. The trick is having specific stories and numbers ready before you sit down — and that's exactly what an AI assistant is good at when you give it the right inputs. In fifteen minutes, you can walk into a room with three lists ready: questions they'll probably ask, talking points for each, and questions you'll ask them. It can draft the prep, but it can't read the room or know which story from your past will actually land — that's still on you.

## Before you start
- **An AI assistant you already use** — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, or any other chat-style assistant. The steps are the same.
- **The full job description** copied to your clipboard. Don't paraphrase yet; the more detail the assistant sees, the sharper the output.
- **A short paragraph about you** — your current role, years of experience, and one or two wins you'd actually mention in an interview.
- **About 15 minutes** — enough time to do the back-and-forth and skim the result.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh chat and name it after the role
Click **New chat** (or **New conversation** — look for a pencil-and-paper icon or a **+** sign) in your assistant. Before you type anything, give the chat a name you'll recognize later, like "Acme Senior Designer interview" or just the company plus the role.

**Why a new chat?** Older messages from unrelated work can leak in and confuse the assistant. A fresh, named thread keeps everything you build here tied to this one interview — easy to find the night before, easy to revisit if a second round is scheduled.

💬 Example: name it "Acme – Marketing Lead interview prep."

You'll know it worked when a new empty chat opens with the name you chose (or with an editable title field at the top of the screen).

## Step 2 — Paste the job description and your background in one message
In your new chat, send a single message that contains two clearly labeled blocks: the job description, and a paragraph about you. Use clear labels like **"JOB POSTING:"** and **"ABOUT ME:"** so the assistant knows where one ends and the other begins. Very long descriptions (over a few thousand words) may need to be split into two messages if your app refuses the paste.

**What happens next:** the assistant usually replies with a short acknowledgement ("Got it — ready when you are") or jumps straight into a summary. Either is fine.

**If it looks different:** if pasting a long posting fails, try uploading the posting as a file — most assistants accept PDFs and text files in the same chat where you usually send text.

💬 Example:

```
JOB POSTING:
[Paste the full job description here — responsibilities, requirements, and any "nice to haves"]

ABOUT ME:
[Paste 4–6 sentences: current role, years of experience, two recent achievements with numbers if you have them]
```

You'll know it worked when the assistant confirms it has the context — usually with a brief recap, a clarifying question, or simply by being ready to answer your next prompt.

## Step 3 — Ask for ten likely interview questions
Send a single, specific prompt asking for ten questions the hiring manager is likely to ask, based on what you just pasted. Ask for a mix of categories — behavioral, technical, and situational — so the list isn't one-note.

**Why ten?** Fewer than that and you may miss the ones that come up. More than ten and you'll feel overloaded. Ten is the sweet spot: enough to practice, small enough to actually read.

💬 Example: "Based on the job posting and my background above, give me ten interview questions a hiring manager is most likely to ask me. Mix behavioral, technical, and situational questions. For each, add one sentence on what they're really trying to find out."

**If it looks different:** if the list comes back generic, follow up with "make these specific to [the company or team from the posting]" and ask for a fresh list. A vague list is usually a sign the original prompt needed more context, not a sign the assistant is broken.

You'll know it worked when you have a numbered list of ten specific, role-tied questions — not stock ones like "tell me about yourself."

## Step 4 — Get two concrete talking points for each question
Without starting a new chat, follow up with a second prompt asking for two concrete talking points under each of the ten questions. Ask for stories, examples, or numbers drawn from your own background — and tell the assistant to flag any question where your pasted background looks thin and you'll need to dig deeper yourself.

**What happens next:** the assistant writes a structured answer, often with a short headline per question and a couple of ideas underneath. This is the moment the prep actually becomes useful.

**If it looks different:** if the response is too long to scan, add "keep each talking point to two sentences max" in your next prompt, or ask it to rewrite the same list more concisely.

💬 Example: "Now for each of those ten questions, give me two concrete talking points I could use, drawing from my background. Keep each point to one or two sentences. Flag any question where my pasted background seems thin."

You'll know it worked when each of the ten questions now has two short, specific points you could picture yourself saying out loud.

## Step 5 — Ask for five smart questions to ask back
In the same chat, ask for five questions you, the candidate, should ask the interviewer. Ask for ones that show you did your homework — about the team, the goals, or how the role is measured. The point is to leave the conversation with real signals, not rehearsed fluff.

💬 Example: "Give me five strong questions I, the candidate, can ask back at the end of the interview. Make them specific to this role and company. Skip anything generic like 'what's the culture like'."

**If it looks different:** if any of the questions come back feeling templated, follow up with "replace any you can't tailor to this exact role" — most assistants will rewrite them on the spot.

You'll know it worked when you have five questions you wouldn't have thought of on your own, and each one is something you'd genuinely want answered.

## Step 6 — Pin or save the chat and skim the highlights
Take thirty seconds to skim the chat and star, pin, or copy the talking points that felt most true to you. Different apps handle this differently — look for a **star icon** next to an answer, a **pin** option in a menu, or just copy the best points into a notes app where you'll actually see them again.

**Why bother?** Two reasons. First, you'll want to reread the chat the morning of the interview. Second, picking the strongest two or three talking points now means you practice those — not all twenty.

**If it looks different:** if your assistant has no pin or star option, the chat's title alone usually makes it easy to find later. Or paste the talking points into your phone's notes app under the company name.

💬 Example: pick the talking points that felt truest to your real work — maybe one about leadership, one about a measurable result, one about a hard problem you solved — and re-read them once before you walk into the interview.

You'll know it worked when you can open the chat or your notes in under ten seconds and find the three talking points you actually plan to use.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting only the company blurb.** If the description is six paragraphs long and you paste just the first one, the assistant's questions will be vague. Paste the whole thing — responsibilities, requirements, and any "nice to haves" — so the assistant has the full picture.
- **Asking for "interview questions" without context.** A generic request gets generic answers. Always include both the job description and your background in the same chat; that's what makes the list specific to *this* role and *your* level.
- **Stopping after the first list.** The ten questions are the start, not the end. The follow-up that asks for talking points is where the real prep happens. Skip it and you'll have a list of questions with nothing ready to say.
- **Treating the output as a script.** The assistant may suggest a story you don't actually have. Treat the talking points as a draft, not a script — swap in your own real examples whenever you can.
- **Reusing the same chat for unrelated work.** Once you start mixing topics, the assistant's answers drift. Keep this chat dedicated to one interview until you're done with it.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same recipe works for any "I have a document and I want to be ready" moment — a school presentation, a doctor's appointment where you want a list of questions, or a tough conversation with a landlord. Paste the source, share your context, ask for what you need.
- **For your business or work:** if you ever sit on the other side of the table, paste the job description and a candidate's resume into the same flow and you'll get a quick read on likely strengths, gaps, and good first-round questions — useful when screening applications.
- **If you want to go further:** the next level is saving this whole structure as a **Custom Instruction** or a saved template in your assistant, so the next time you prep, you only paste the job posting and your background — the rest of the structure is already loaded. Many assistants also let you create a dedicated "Project" or named workspace for one company, so multiple chats (prep, follow-up, salary research) live together.

## Try it now
Open a new chat in the assistant you already use, name it after a real interview you have coming up (or one you're imagining), and paste one real job description plus four sentences about your background. Then send the prompt from Step 3. Ten minutes from now, you'll have a list you didn't have ten minutes ago.
